sources.news_title: Speaker Johnson Cancels Thursday House Session, Pushing Hegseth Impeachment Vote Until After Midterms
sources.text:
House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA) announced he has canceled a planned House session for Thursday, sending lawmakers for an early seven-week recess and pushing back a vote to impeach US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth until after the midterm elections.
Rep. Thomas Massie (R-KY), who introduced the resolution to impeach Hegseth, suspected Johnson might take drastic measures to avoid the vote, so he didn’t inform GOP leadership of his plan to introduce the resolution, which he did on the House floor on Tuesday.
“And there it is. Just as I predicted. They’re canceling Congress tomorrow to avoid the vote on IMPEACHING [Hegseth]. It will also make it harder for us to reach 218 signatures on the Epstein Discharge Petition before the election. We were at 190+ signatures last night,” Massie wrote on X after Johnson canceled the votes.
While Johnson didn’t explicitly say the Hegseth impeachment was the reason for canceling Thursday’s votes, Reese Gorman, a reporter for The Washington Sun, reported right before the cancellation was official that some in House leadership “want to avoid a vote on the Hegseth impeachment set to come up tomorrow since it’s privileged.”
Johnson’s move also came after seven House Republicans voted against the Iran war by voting in favor of a War Powers Resolution that would direct President Trump to end the conflict. The bill passed 220-204, with all 213 Democrats present voting in favor.
The House has held multiple votes on the Iran war, but the Tuesday night vote had the highest number of Republicans supporting a resolution to end the conflict, signaling that Massie may get some Republican support over the Hegseth impeachment since it’s centered on the conflict with Iran.
Both the House and the Senate have already passed a concurrent Iran War Powers Resolution, which, under the 1973 War Powers Act, should direct the president to remove US forces from hostilities with Iran.
Massie argued in his eight articles of impeachment for Hegseth that passing the concurrent War Powers Resolution was one of the multiple ways Hegseth and the administration are breaking the law by continuing the Iran war.
The articles also address how Hegseth has ignored US laws designed to mitigate civilian casualties, his role in extrajudicial executions at sea (strikes on alleged drug-running boats), the attack on Venezuela to abduct President Maduro, the bombing campaign in Yemen last year, and his efforts to chill free speech.

sources.news_title: Speaker Johnson recesses the House early as Rep. Thomas Massie pushes Hegseth impeachment – WTOP News
sources.text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Speaker Mike Johnson is closing up the House early, sending lawmakers home Wednesday to campaign for the midterm elections after what he claims is the most productive Congress in decades.
But not without a scathing rebuke from GOP Rep. Thomas Massie for all the unfinished business.
Massie’s resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over the war in Iran and his bipartisan effort to force the release of more files in the Jeffrey Epstein investigation are all being left behind, blocked from votes.
“We’re calling off Congress? And we’re in the majority?” Massie railed from the House floor.
“I’m trying to get justice for the Epstein survivors,” he said. “I’m trying to stop a war.”
Massie, the renegade Republican from Kentucky, seized control of the chamber for a blistering hourlong speech criticizing Johnson, the Republican majority and the work he said the speaker is refusing to conduct to lower prices for Americans and hold the Trump administration accountable.
“Why would we be canceling days when the country is burning?” Massie said. “We should stay here for every day that’s on the calendar and we should debate.”
A fitting end to a tumultuous House session
The afternoon showdown provided a colorful capstone to what has been a tumultuous two-year session of House Republicans in control by a bare majority, with Johnson routinely struggling to keep the place running.
Despite the enormous tools of the gavel — the speaker holds one of the most powerful positions in Washington, second in the line of succession to the president — Johnson has often been thwarted by his own conference.
The speaker has repeatedly and abruptly canceled House voting days to send lawmakers home rather than manage the disruptions from his own rebellious flank — particularly those legislative efforts that threatened to rebuke President Donald Trump.
By one tally, the House has cut 28 days this year, while adding four others, for a net loss of 24 days — about one-fourth of the total scheduled.
Still, Johnson has hauled major legislation to the finish line, most notably the “Big Beautiful Bill,” a package of tax breaks and social service cuts that Trump signed into law last summer. And on Wednesday the House powered through a full agenda, passing bills large and small, including one to name the American mastodon the national fossil mammal and the Tyrannosaurus Rex the national fossil dinosaur.
Johnson called Massie’s effort to impeach Hegseth “a stunt.”
“Secretary Hegseth has done an extraordinary job at the Department of War,” Johnson said.
“This has literally been the most productive and successful and aggressive Congress” in decades, he said earlier this month, calling it the top five of all time. “We’re confident American voters are going to remember that when they head to vote this fall.”
Voters will be assessing the situation in November as they decide whether to keep Trump’s party in power, while Democrats work to dislodge Republicans from majority control of both the House and the Senate.
House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries assailed the “do-nothing” Republican majority and promised Democrats will perform better.
“Donald Trump and MAGA Republicans promised to bring down grocery prices on Day One. They promised to stop endless wars in the Middle East,” Jeffries said from the steps of the Capitol, flanked by Democratic lawmakers.
“But Republicans have done nothing to make life more affordable for the American people,” he said.
He said Democrats’ message is a simple one: “We hear you. We see you … And we are committed to making life better for you.”
Massie’s last stand
The confrontation also provided a platform for Massie, the libertarian-leaning go-his-own-way congressman who orchestrated the initial release of the Epstein files and helped lead efforts to halt the conflict in Iran through a war powers resolution.
Massie lost his own primary bid for reelection after Trump mounted a costly campaign to kick him out of Congress.
But the congressman has only appeared emboldened in his final days in office.
Massie spent much of his floor speech assailing Johnson’s leadership and decrying what he calls the “uniparty,” which he characterizes as moving in lockstep with big-money special interests at home and abroad.
He also devoted substantial time to criticizing Hegseth and the “stupid war” he said the U.S. should not be involved with in Iran. Deriding Hegseth’s leadership, he mocked the secretary for trying to rename the Defense Department as the Department of War without consulting Congress.
“Hell, you can’t even rename a post office without us,” he said.
Hegseth’s role in sending the U.S. into the Iran wars without approval of Congress and directing the U.S.’s military strikes of alleged drug trafficking boats in the Caribbean are among the actions Massie characterized as high crimes and misdemeanors in the articles of impeachment against the Defense secretary.
Massie said he knew when he landed in Washington that he would stand apart.
“I’m not playing this game,” he said. “I am going to tell people what is going on up here.”

Johnson Sends House Home, Blocks Massie Hegseth Impeachment
sources.text:
Speaker Mike Johnson cut the House session short and sent members home for a seven-week recess, a move that shelves a forced floor vote on Rep. Thomas Massie's impeachment resolution against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth until after the November midterms.
Johnson told reporters Wednesday that the early adjournment had nothing to do with the impeachment push from the Kentucky Republican, who had spent hours reading his 34-page resolution aloud on the House floor. The Speaker framed the departure as routine pre-election business, saying members needed time in their districts ahead of competitive midterm races.
But the timing is hard to ignore. Massie's resolution carried special procedural powers, a privileged designation that forced House leaders to act within two legislative days. By clearing the chamber early, Johnson ran out the clock. The impeachment vote now sits on ice until members return after November.
Massie did not give Republican leadership advance warning. He deliberately concealed the impeachment articles from party leaders before reading them on the House floor, Just The News reported.
Massie explained why in blunt terms:
"I was afraid that they would do something to subvert me getting on the floor for an hour and 20 minutes and reading these articles."
The maneuver worked, at least long enough for Massie to get his arguments on the record. But it also guaranteed a hostile reception from leadership. Johnson dismissed the entire effort as grandstanding.
"It is a publicity stunt by someone who wants attention," Johnson told reporters. "It will immediately be tabled of course. But we probably won't do that today, we will do it when we come back."
Johnson added: "We should not be playing games with national security."
Massie's resolution laid out eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth. The central charge accused the Defense Secretary of violating the War Powers Resolution of 1973, the federal law requiring congressional authorization for military operations lasting longer than 90 days, by continuing to prosecute the Iran conflict without that authorization. The New York Post noted that the Iran war began February 28, and that both the House and Senate had passed resolutions calling on President Trump to end it, despite Republicans controlling both chambers.
The resolution went beyond Iran. Massie accused the Pentagon of kidnapping then-President Nicolás Maduro of Venezuela "under the guise of narcotics law enforcement, though in actuality intended to assert U.S. control over Venezuela's oil reserves." Additional charges covered military operations in Yemen, strikes on alleged drug boats, accusations that Hegseth ignored laws requiring the military to minimize civilian casualties, and claims of suppressing free speech by retaliating against critics of the administration, the Washington Examiner reported.
Massie's resolution stated that Hegseth "has demonstrated that he will remain a threat to the Constitution if allowed to remain in office, and has acted in a manner grossly incompatible with his duties and the rule of law."
Pentagon press secretary Kingsley Wilson pushed back, saying "the entire Department is unified behind the Secretary's vision and will continue working to put our warfighters and America first."
The administration did not wait for the House vote to mount a defense. On Tuesday, Attorney General Todd Blanche held a press briefing in the White House Rose Garden specifically to back the Defense Secretary.
"Secretary Hegseth is doing a phenomenal job, and the secretary of war doesn't just go off and do things. So, he follows the law. And so the DOJ plays a role in that, and we play an active role in making sure the laws are complied with."
The White House also argued that the Iran conflict's initial phase of fighting had ended, resetting the 90-day clock under the War Powers Resolution, and that the resolution itself unconstitutionally constrains presidential authority over foreign policy. Courts have historically declined to enforce the War Powers Resolution's timeline, a legal reality that undercuts Massie's strongest charge.
Massie is not running for reelection. He lost his primary to a Trump-backed opponent, making him a lame-duck congressman with nothing left to lose politically, and, his critics would argue, nothing left to gain except attention. That context matters. A sitting Republican member filing impeachment articles against a cabinet secretary in his own party's administration is extraordinary. A lame-duck member doing it seven weeks before midterms, after hiding the resolution from his own leadership, looks less like a principled stand and more like a parting shot.
Massie has framed the effort as a constitutional obligation. He pointed to the House's repeated votes to end the Iran conflict, three times now, and argued that Hegseth's continued prosecution of the war without fresh congressional authorization amounts to lawbreaking.
House Democrats had already introduced their own six articles of impeachment against Hegseth back in April. Massie's resolution, filed from the Republican side of the aisle, added bipartisan weight to the war-powers debate even as it stood no realistic chance of advancing.
House Republicans were already in a sour mood before Massie's stunt. Members faced political pressure on multiple fronts, AI policy, tariffs, and midterm anxiety, and were eager to get home to campaign. Johnson's decision to move the departure up by a day, from Thursday to Wednesday evening, gave the conference what it wanted while conveniently disposing of the impeachment clock.
The last votes Wednesday evening were on a Russia sanctions bill described as a major White House priority. After that, members scattered for a seven-week stretch that will keep them away from Washington until after the November elections.
Johnson made clear the impeachment resolution will be tabled, procedurally killed, the moment the House reconvenes. That outcome was never in doubt. Republicans hold the majority, and there is no appetite within the conference to impeach a sitting Defense Secretary over war-powers disputes that courts have historically refused to adjudicate.
The war-powers question Massie raised is a legitimate constitutional debate, and it deserves serious engagement from Congress. But a lame-duck member ambushing his own party's leadership with a privileged resolution he hid until the last minute is not serious engagement, it is a procedural grenade tossed on the way out the door. Johnson was right to call it what it was and move on.

House Speaker Johnson sends Congress home early, delaying Hegseth impeachment vote
WASHINGTON (CNN) – House Speaker Mike Johnson said Wednesday he is sending lawmakers home early for their seven-week midterm campaign recess.
“The House has done its work. You’ve seen the statistics we’ve been talking about for the last few days. This House has been the second-most productive in terms of legislation in the history of the institution since 1789. We passed over 900 pieces of legislation,” Johnson said.
The move will delay a forced vote on impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth until after the November elections.
Republican Rep. Thomas Massie introduced the resolution over Hegseth’s handling of the U.S. war with Iran.
Massie accuses Hegseth of abusing his authority and carrying out unlawful orders.
Johnson called the effort a “publicity stunt” and said the early departure has nothing to do with Hegseth.
“That’s ridiculous. It’s a publicity stunt by someone who wants attention. It will immediately be tabled, of course, but we probably won’t do that today. We’ll probably do it when we come back, but it’s a stunt. Secretary Hegseth has done an extraordinary job at the Department of War. We’re in the middle of international conflicts right now and we should not be playing games with national security, and I think that’s how the members see this,” Johnson said.
House Republicans had planned to remain in session until Thursday, but will now take their final votes Wednesday night.

sources.news_title: House delays Hegseth impeachment vote until November
sources.text:
WASHINGTON — The House will not vote on an effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth until November after Republican leaders on Wednesday canceled the chamber’s last day of work before a lengthy recess.
Speaker Mike Johnson said he is sending members home a day early to give them a head start on campaigning for the midterm elections. The change in the legislative schedule means there will be no vote Thursday on the impeachment, as had been expected.
Republican Thomas Massie of Kentucky said he had predicted the move after introducing articles of impeachment against Hegseth on Tuesday, accusing him of “high crimes and misdemeanors” for unlawfully waging war against Iran.
“They’re canceling Congress tomorrow to avoid the vote on IMPEACHING @SecWar,” he wrote on X.
The resolution is privileged, meaning the House must vote on it within two legislative days under chamber rules.
Johnson, R-La., on Wednesday morning dismissed Massie’s attempt to oust Hegseth as a “publicity stunt by someone who wants attention.”
“It will immediately be tabled, of course. But we probably won’t do that today. We will do it when we come back,” Johnson told reporters. “But it’s a stunt. Secretary Hegseth has done an extraordinary job at the Department of War.”
On Tuesday, the House tabled the latest bid by Rep. Al Green, D-Texas, to impeach President Donald Trump over the administration’s immigration crackdown.
Massie on Wednesday afternoon railed in a floor speech against Johnson and his decision to cancel Thursday votes. The impeachment vote would have been “real easy,” he said.
“It’d be probably be a vote to table, to insulate the members of this body from any accountability,” he said. “That would avoid you from having to debate the issue, any of the eight articles of impeachment.”
In addition to the Iran war, Massie’s 34-page resolution charges Hegseth with ignoring laws to minimize civilian casualties, carrying out extrajudicial killings by striking suspected drug boats and suppressing free speech by seeking to discipline Democratic Sen. Mark Kelly of Arizona for telling troops they can refuse illegal orders.
The resolution also accuses Hegseth of kidnapping former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife from Venezuela without constitutional or legal authority and for initiating unlawful strikes on Yemen that caused extensive civilian deaths.
A Pentagon spokesperson on Tuesday defended Hegseth, calling him a “transformative leader” and saying the department is unified behind his leadership.
A group of nine Democrats introduced an impeachment resolution against Hegseth in April, but Massie’s measure stands out because it targets a Cabinet member from his own party.
Massie is set to leave the House in January after losing his primary in May to former Navy SEAL Ed Gallrein. Hegseth had campaigned for Gallrein, accusing Massie of “too much grandstanding, too few great votes.”
The House is scheduled to return to Washington on Nov. 9, following the midterm elections.

sources.news_title: House Set to Leave Early, Won’t Return Until After Midterms
sources.text:
House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) has canceled votes after Sept. 16 and will send members home earlier than expected for a recess that won’t end until after the November midterm elections.
The House was scheduled to remain in session until Oct. 1. Johnson did not provide a reason for the cancellation. Johnson told reporters on Sept. 16 that the House has done its job passing bills and that most of them await Senate action.
Johnson’s decision came amid the introduction of an impeachment resolution and the issue of artificial intelligence taking center stage on Capitol Hill.
“Secretary Hegseth has acted in a manner contrary to his trust as Secretary of Defense and subversive of constitutional government, to the great prejudice of the cause of law and justice, and to the manifest injury of the people of the United States of America,” Massie said on the House floor.
The resolution would have required a vote no later than Thursday. Recessing early stalls a vote. Johnson said there will be a motion to table it when the House returns from recess.
The Senate is scheduled to remain in session until Oct. 2.
The upcoming recess also comes amid calls for Congress to take up the issue of regulating artificial intelligence. Johnson has resisted immediate calls to regulate AI in favor of a balanced approach.
“They can self-regulate. They don’t need the government to tell them to slow it down. If they want to slow it down, they should,” Johnson told reporters on Sept. 15. “We cannot have a moratorium on the development of AI, OK? Because then we will lose our edge to China, and that has serious national security implications for every American family.”
A letter from more than 100 House Democrats called on Johnson to keep the House in session to pass safeguards for artificial intelligence.
“Reasonable minds may disagree about precisely how Congress should regulate this rapidly evolving technology,” they wrote on Sept. 15. “We cannot disagree about the imperative for Congress to act.”
In response to the letter, Johnson’s office referred The Epoch Times to comments Johnson made on Sept. 15.
“We do not want to jump in—the reflex of legislative bodies is to cover things up with red tape and hyperregulation,” he told reporters. “If you do that, then you lose your edge, and that is a national security concern for the American people … we will strike the right balance, but we are not going to act irrationally or haphazardly because that could have negative secondary effects.”
The House is scheduled today to vote on a bill to sanction Russia and Iran. The legislation would impose sanctions on the five countries that are the biggest purchasers of oil and gas from Russia. It also looks to stop Russia from using oil and gas sales to fund its war against Ukraine, which started in February 2022.
On Tuesday, two Democrats, Maine Rep. Jared Golden and Washington Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, voted with 211 Republicans to advance legislation that included the bill to sanction Russia and Iran. This was the second time since Sept. 1 that the legislators voted with Republicans on a procedural vote.
The lower congressional chamber is also expected to vote on a measure that would establish the National Fraud Enforcement Division within the Department of Justice. A bill to “enhance information-sharing capabilities between federal law enforcement and state agencies to detect, investigate, and prosecute fraud in certain federal programs, and to protect individual privacy” is also set to get a vote.
Additionally, the House is scheduled to vote on the Ratepayer Protection Act, which seeks to prevent taxpayers from being financially responsible for the costs associated with data centers.
In addition to the Ratepayer Protection Act, the House is expected to vote on bills that would require a two-thirds vote.

sources.news_title: House departs for midterms early as Speaker Johnson disses Massie's impeachment 'stunt'
sources.text:
WASHINGTON — House Speaker Mike Johnson moved one vote originally planned for Thursday to Wednesday evening, allowing lawmakers to leave Washington a day early for the midterm election recess.
A spokesman for Johnson’s office told RightLine the chamber was not canceling its remaining business. Leadership finished the scheduled work faster and shifted that single pre-planned vote up so members could depart Wednesday night instead of remaining for a Thursday session.
Johnson told reporters the House had completed its work and that members should return to their districts.
“The House has done its work,” Johnson said. “It’s time for our members to go home to their districts and make their case to the American people.”
He said the House has passed more than 900 bills this Congress, with about 700 awaiting action in the Senate. This week alone, he said, the chamber would pass more than 70 measures, including the Ratepayer Protection Act, a Russia sanctions bill, Congressional Review Act resolutions and anti-fraud legislation.
“A lot of it is just awaiting action in the Senate,” Johnson said.
The earlier departure also means the House will not take up a privileged impeachment resolution filed Tuesday by Kentucky Rep. Thomas Massie against Secretary of War Pete Hegseth. That measure was not part of the pre-planned Thursday agenda. Because it was filed as privileged business, it would have required action within two legislative days, setting up a potential vote Thursday if the House had remained in session.
Johnson dismissed Massie’s filing as a “publicity stunt by someone who wants attention” and said it would be tabled when the House returns after the election.
“Secretary Hegseth has done an extraordinary job at the Department of War,” Johnson said. “We’re in the middle of international conflicts right now, and we should not be playing games with national security.”
Massie has argued Hegseth continued the war with Iran beyond the 60-day limit in the War Powers Resolution without authorization from Congress. The House has voted multiple times on measures to end the conflict, but none has reached President Donald Trump with enough support to overcome a veto.
House members are not expected back for floor votes until after the Nov. 3 midterm elections. All 435 House seats are on the ballot.

Massie also accused Hegseth of carrying out extrajudicial killings by bombing boats in the Caribbean Sea, suppressing free speech by retaliating against Democratic Sen. Mark Kelly of Arizona for urging troops not to follow illegal orders, and kidnapping former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro.
House rules say that the speaker has to put the articles of impeachment on the floor for a vote within two legislative days. That clearly terrifies Republicans, as it would force them to either defy Trump by impeaching his favorite warmonger or tacitly vote to support the wildly unpopular war in Iran.
Both of those are bad options for Republicans, who can’t afford to anger Trump ahead of the midterms. But voting against the impeachment would essentially be signing off on how he’s handled the Iran war.
So rather than putting Republicans in that position, House Speaker Mike Johnson called a recess to stop the clock on the two-day voting rule.
Related | Things almost couldn’t be worse for Republicans
“I think it shows the cowardice of the Republican Party,” Democratic Rep. Pramila Jayapal of Washington said. “They are canceling votes to do business for the American people because they are afraid that that impeachment resolution of Pete Hegseth would pass on a bipartisan basis.”
She concluded, “The American people deserve better than Pete Hegseth and Donald Trump.”
Johnson had already canceled two weeks of votes that were scheduled through the end of September, saying that Republicans needed to get back to their districts to campaign. But campaigning for the next 48 days is unlikely to save them anyway.
Trump’s war in Iran and capitulation to Russia in its war against Ukraine have spiked oil prices, raising the cost of fuel across the globe. And that will have downstream inflationary impacts, as diesel—which is used to transport goods and power farming machinery—is at a record high.
Oil and gas experts say that prices are not going to come down in the near future, sounding the alarm on potential fuel shortages.
And it’s all happening just as voters tune in to the general election, with early voting having already started in a handful of states, with more set to come online in the coming days.
We’re already seeing voters’ frustration impacting polls, with Democrats surging on the generic ballot and leading in critical House and Senate races in regions that Trump carried by double digits in 2024.
Since Sept. 1, Democrats’ lead on the generic ballot has grown by 1.1 points, with Marquette University Law School releasing a poll Wednesday that shows Democrats with a 13-point lead among likely voters. If it comes to fruition, that would be an extinction-level election for the GOP.
So House Republicans can go home to campaign all they want. But when they return, many of them will be losers.

WASHINGTON ― House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) has canceled Thursday’s votes and will instead send members home early, making Tuesday’s business in the House the last before the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
Johnson, who already canceled the next two weeks of the legislative session, told reporters the House had been incredibly productive all year and didn’t need to stick around another day.
“It’s time for our members to go home to their districts and make their case to the American people to go and explain all the great things we’ve done,” Johnson said.
Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.), however, told reporters Tuesday he expected leadership to cancel votes because he’d introduced a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Rank-and-file members have the power to force votes on such resolutions, and Massie planned to do so. When a member invokes his privilege to force a vote, the House has to act within two legislative days, though leadership can set a vote to table the resolution instead of a vote on the resolution itself.
“I do expect it’ll cancel Congress,” Massie said Tuesday. “But that won’t get Peter Hegseth out of the noose, so to speak. We come back after the election, and it would be the same members of Congress” who will have to vote on the resolution.
Among other things, the resolution says Hegseth committed high crimes and misdemeanors for prosecuting the war in Iran without congressional authorization and suppressed free speech by retaliating against Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) for participating in a video reminding members of the military not to follow unlawful orders.
Johnson called Massie’s contention “ridiculous” in response to a reporter’s question on Wednesday.
“It’s a publicity stunt by someone who wants attention. It will immediately be tabled, of course, but we probably won’t do that today. We’ll probably do it when we come back,” Johnson said. “But it’s a stunt. Secretary Hegseth has done an extraordinary job at the Department of War. We’re in the middle of international conflicts right now, and we should not be playing games with national security.”
Massie pointed out Johnson sent lawmakers home for their August recess two weeks early last July amid a furor over the Donald Trump administration’s then-refusal to release its files on Jeffrey Epstein. He said he kept his Hegseth impeachment plans to himself as a result.

One Republican rages against House’s early exit
In rare use of ‘personal privilege,’ Massie rebukes House cancellation of votes
As the House heads home early this week with no plans to return until November, at least one Republican isn’t happy about it.
In a rare use of members’ “personal privilege,” Rep. Thomas Massie continued a feud with Speaker Mike Johnson, who earlier this month accused the Kentucky Republican of “not participating as a full member of the Congress.”
House procedure allows members to raise questions of personal privilege on the floor to respond to criticism of their integrity as elected representatives, but they have seldom taken advantage of it in recent years.
“I’m here today to let you know that I’m a full participating member of the House of Representatives. In fact, when other people want to go home, I’m here to work. I’m here to get justice for the Epstein victims, the survivors. I am here to get the price of food and fuel down for our constituents. We’ve got solutions. We just refuse to pass them,” he said on the House floor Wednesday as he raged against his own party.
Massie spent an hour on the House floor Wednesday afternoon lambasting the House’s truncated schedule and suggesting leaders were trying to leave town so they wouldn’t have to deal with his quests for transparency and accountability — namely his latest effort to require the Justice Department to release more files related to the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and his push to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
Earlier in the day, House leaders announced they would cancel votes on Thursday — a decision that came after Johnson had already lopped two weeks off the House schedule that had been planned for later in September, as members return to their districts to campaign ahead of the midterms.
A discharge petition launched by Massie in September to bring another Epstein-related bill to the House floor, dubbed the Epstein Files Transparency Act II, is nearing the required 218 signatures. The biggest obstacle for Massie is Republican support of his effort. If every House Democrat signs the petition, he’ll need one more Republican.
As of Wednesday afternoon, the only Republicans who had signed were Massie and Reps. Nancy Mace, R-S.C., and Ralph Norman, R-S.C. None of those three will be returning to Congress next year, with Massie losing his primary to a challenger backed by President Donald Trump and Mace and Norman both falling short in their unsuccessful bids for South Carolina governor.
The bill would allow state attorneys general, victims and members of Congress to sue the Justice Department for failing to disclose documents as required under the law he championed last fall.
And he’s not the only Republican unhappy — Norman called the canceled votes “unacceptable” on X Wednesday afternoon.
“The House has now canceled at least 63 scheduled voting days this Congress, including nine days this month alone, and now we’re leaving Washington until after the election. The Founders did not envision taking this much time off and still getting paid. If Members of Congress want to go home and campaign instead of doing the job taxpayers sent us here to do, then their campaigns ought to be paying them, NOT the American taxpayer,” he wrote.
Massie’s first attempt to force the Justice Department to release Epstein files, which he led alongside Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., easily passed the House after a battle to bring it to the floor against the wishes of leadership. It was signed into law last November.
“What would a fully participating member of Congress do if he got a law enacted against the will of the president, against the will of the speaker … against all odds, and then the chief law enforcement officer of the country will not follow the law? What would a fully participating member of Congress do? Well, I think he’d do what I did,” Massie said.
Massie is hoping to make the most of his limited time left in Congress. “I’m going to do something every week, so that I won’t be sitting at home saying, ‘I wish I’d done that,’” he said in June.
Some, however, took umbrage at Massie’s actions.
“Sadly we have Members of Congress who didn’t get picked by their 5th Grade Kickball Team and are taking out their frustration on the institution of the House of Representatives. #MoveOn,” Rep. Greg Murphy, R-N.C., wrote on X Wednesday as Massie’s floor speech went on.
Massie doesn’t see it the same way.
“Why would we be canceling days when the country is burning? The inflation is rampant. There are things we could do here. Why would we cancel our own majority?” he said.
Jackie Wang contributed to this report.

sources.text:
(WASHINGTON) — Outgoing Republican Rep. Thomas Massie seized the House floor for more than an hour Tuesday afternoon, launching a long-shot effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth stemming from his controversial administration over the Pentagon, including the war in Iran.
After sending a news release announcing his intent to impeach Hegseth, Massie quickly appeared on the floor where he stood for more than 67 minutes reading the sweeping 34-page resolution with eight articles of impeachment aloud.
“Secretary Hegseth has acted in a manner contrary to his trust as Secretary of Defense and subversive of constitutional government, to the great prejudice of the cause of law and justice, and to the manifest injury of the people of the United States of America,” Massie read from the resolution, contending that Hegseth will “remain a threat to civilians and the laws of war, the integrity of United States diplomacy, and the Constitution if allowed to remain in office, and has acted in a manner grossly incompatible with his duties and the rule of law.”
“Peter Brian Hegseth thus warrants impeachment and trial, removal from office, and disqualification to hold and enjoy any office of honor, trust, or profit under the United States,” the resolution states.
The Pentagon responded to Massie’s move, defending Hegseth in a statement to ABC News.
“Secretary Hegseth has been a transformative leader for the Department of War,” Pentagon press secretary Kingsley Wilson said in the statement, later adding that the “entire Department is unified behind the Secretary’s vision and will continue working to put our warfighters and America first.”
The articles of impeachment against Hegseth include ignoring laws that minimize civilian casualties, administering an “unlawful war” in Yemen, ordering extrajudicial killings, suppressing free speech and kidnapping a sovereign leader — alluding to the U.S. capture of Nicolas Maduro early this year.
“Frankly, I was concerned that Mike Johnson would end Congress again, like shorten even our already truncated work period if he found out I was doing this. So I shared the idea with nobody,” Massie said.
Massie, a conservative who has gained a reputation as a constitutionalist through his seven terms in the House, lost a primary earlier this summer after Trump endorsed his opponent.
It’s unclear whether the vote will succeed, given Republicans’ narrow majority in the House. Speaker Mike Johnson can lose two Republican votes before a third defection upsets the majority.
Unless GOP leaders change the floor schedule again, the House must hold a vote on the resolution within two-legislative days — by Thursday, which would force Republicans to go on the record defending Hegseth ahead of the high-stakes midterm elections. GOP leaders could offer a motion to table the resolution or cancel the legislative session scheduled for Thursday to avoid the vote.
Speaking to reporters afterward, Massie explained that he introduced the articles of impeachment to place a “marker” in history on what he said was both President Donald Trump’s and Hegseth’s “illegal” conduct.
“Doing this wasn’t predicated on whether it could succeed or not; there needs to be a marker in history,” Massie said. “The president has exceeded, and Secretary Hegseth specifically, in many ways himself, and sometimes directed by illegal orders from the president, they have exceeded all norms for rules of engagement for how you use or misuse our military, to take oil from another country, to kidnap a foreign leader, like somebody needs to put a marker in history, and that’s what this is. Hopefully, it passes, and they can litigate this in the Senate.”
Massie also told ABC News he had waited until Tuesday because it presents the last possible time to force consideration of a privileged resolution Congress before the midterms.
Massie added he felt he had exhausted all other legislative ways to stymie the war in Iran as well as other foreign military interventions.
“Why today? Because Speaker Johnson has basically canceled the rest of Congress until the elections,” Massie explained. “Two days from now is the end of our session before we go on recess, and there can be a vote within two days. So I had to do it today.”

WASHINGTON (AP) — Speaker Mike Johnson is closing up the House early, sending lawmakers home Wednesday to campaign for the midterm elections after what he claims is the most productive Congress in decades.
But not without a scathing rebuke from GOP Rep. Thomas Massie for all the unfinished business.
Massie’s resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over the war in Iran and his bipartisan effort to force the release of more files in the Jeffrey Epstein investigation are all being left behind, blocked from votes.
“We’re calling off Congress? And we’re in the majority?” Massie railed from the House floor.
“I’m trying to get justice for the Epstein survivors,” he said. “I’m trying to stop a war.”
Massie, the renegade Republican from Kentucky, seized control of the chamber for a blistering hourlong speech criticizing Johnson, the Republican majority and the work he said the speaker is refusing to conduct to lower prices for Americans and hold the Trump administration accountable.
“Why would we be canceling days when the country is burning?” Massie said. “We should stay here for every day that’s on the calendar and we should debate.”
A fitting end to a tumultuous House session
The afternoon showdown provided a colorful capstone to what has been a tumultuous two-year session of House Republicans in control by a bare majority, with Johnson routinely struggling to keep the place running.
Despite the enormous tools of the gavel — the speaker holds one of the most powerful positions in Washington, second in the line of succession to the president — Johnson has often been thwarted by his own conference.
The speaker has repeatedly and abruptly canceled House voting days to send lawmakers home rather than manage the disruptions from his own rebellious flank — particularly those legislative efforts that threatened to rebuke President Donald Trump.
By one tally, the House has cut 28 days this year, while adding four others, for a net loss of 24 days — about one-fourth of the total scheduled.
Still, Johnson has hauled major legislation to the finish line, most notably the “Big Beautiful Bill,” a package of tax breaks and social service cuts that Trump signed into law last summer. And on Wednesday the House powered through a full agenda, passing bills large and small, including one to name the American mastodon the national fossil mammal and the Tyrannosaurus Rex the national fossil dinosaur.
Johnson called Massie’s effort to impeach Hegseth “a stunt.”
“Secretary Hegseth has done an extraordinary job at the Department of War,” Johnson said.
“This has literally been the most productive and successful and aggressive Congress” in decades, he said earlier this month, calling it the top five of all time. “We’re confident American voters are going to remember that when they head to vote this fall.”

House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries assailed the “do-nothing” Republican majority and promised Democrats will perform better.
“Donald Trump and MAGA Republicans promised to bring down grocery prices on Day One. They promised to stop endless wars in the Middle East,” Jeffries said from the steps of the Capitol, flanked by Democratic lawmakers.
“But Republicans have done nothing to make life more affordable for the American people,” he said.

Massie’s last stand

A new report reveals how the federal government paid billions as part of its supposed plan to save taxpayers money.

The federal government paid employees $9.5 billion not to work in 2025 as a result of Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency.

President Trump and Musk’s efforts have shrunk the federal workforce by 12 percent since the inauguration in January last year, but that has not translated into any savings. Of the $9.5 billion figure, $6.7 billion was spent on DOGE’s deferred resignation offer, which about 139,963 federal employees took, resulting in several government departments losing their most experienced personnel. Many departments later scrambled to restaff those positions: The Partnership for Public Service, a nonprofit organization, found that over 20,000 federal jobs vacated by the resignation program have been backfilled. The federal government has also tried to recruit new employees to fill the void, focusing on early-career workers.
“Trump spent billions to push out experienced and badly needed experts across government—this was the most expensive way imaginable to make government worse,” said Democratic Senator Patty Murray in a statement Tuesday.
DOGE was supposed to reduce the size of the federal government and eliminate waste, fraud, and abuse, with Musk promising $1 trillion in savings. Instead, the entire program appears to be a massive example of setting taxpayer dollars on fire.

When he announced the signs to Senators Jeff Merkley and Lisa Murkowski, Burgum said that the “informational signage therefore will provide visitors with important context about the exhibits they are about to encounter and the personal viewpoints that the curators of the exhibits are seeking to advance.”
“We believe the public should enter the museum fully equipped with the information needed to evaluate whether to invest their time in viewing these exhibits and programming,” he wrote in a letter to the senators.
It is not yet clear what exactly the “information needed” will be. The text of the signs or the plans for their physical structure is still undetermined, but Burgam’s letter suggests direct attacks on Smithsonian leaders, including Bunch and museum director Anthea Hartig.

“It is outrageous, beyond the pale, that Republicans sent us on an extended August recess, and now just two weeks later they are cutting Congress short to send us home once again,” said Arizona Representative Yassamin Ansari during a news conference Wednesday morning.
“We just need a few Republicans to stand up to Donald Trump and join us,” House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries concurred. “Instead, they have decided to cancel votes and run out of town without providing any relief to hardworking American taxpayers.”
The House will remain out of session through the month of October and until the midterm elections the month after. Lawmakers will return to session Nov. 9, potentially in a lame-duck Republican Congress. The Senate, for its part, will remain in Washington through Oct. 1.
Recent polling shows Democrats with as much as an 11-point lead over Republicans for control of the House following the midterms. And a New York Times poll published Tuesday suggests some of the shift away from the GOP is thanks to Trump’s unpopularity and the perception that his party is more extreme and more corrupt than Democrats.
If Democrats wrest control of one or both chambers of Congress in November, they’ve vowed to supercharge oversight on the president and his administration.

sources.news_title: House Delays Hegseth Impeachment Vote Until After Midterms
sources.text:
WASHINGTON, United States — Republican leaders abruptly ended voting in the House of Representatives on Wednesday, September 16, 2026, postponing consideration of a resolution to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth until after the November midterm elections.
Votes scheduled for Thursday were cancelled, allowing lawmakers to leave Washington a day earlier than planned.
The House is not scheduled to return until November 9, six days after the elections, according to its legislative calendar.
The decision delays action on a privileged impeachment resolution introduced by Representative Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican, over Hegseth’s conduct as defence secretary.
House Speaker Mike Johnson denied that the schedule change was connected to the impeachment effort.
However, cancelling Thursday’s sitting removed the final legislative day on which the chamber would have been required to consider Massie’s resolution before the election recess.
Privileged Resolution Forced House Action
Massie introduced the measure on Tuesday as a privileged resolution, a designation requiring the House to act within two legislative days.
Republican leaders could have moved to table the resolution, effectively killing it, but doing so would have required lawmakers to cast a politically sensitive recorded vote shortly before the elections.
Johnson called the impeachment effort a “publicity stunt” and said Republican leaders would seek to table it when the House returned.
“Secretary Hegseth has done an extraordinary job,” Johnson told reporters while defending the defence secretary.
Massie’s resolution contains eight articles of impeachment accusing Hegseth of violating federal law and congressional war powers through United States military operations in Iran and elsewhere.
“By engaging in hostilities in Iran for more than 90 days without congressional authorization, Secretary Hegseth is breaking the law and must be held accountable,” Massie said in a statement.
The resolution also accuses Hegseth of disregarding congressional directives, failing to comply with laws intended to limit civilian casualties, authorising extrajudicial military operations, and retaliating against critics of the Trump administration.
The allegations have not been adjudicated, and the Pentagon has defended Hegseth’s leadership.
Republicans Avoid Difficult Pre-Election Vote
Republicans hold a narrow majority in the House and are fighting to retain control of the chamber in the November 3 elections.
A vote on Hegseth could have placed Republican representatives from competitive districts in a difficult position, particularly as public dissatisfaction with the continuing war involving Iran has increased.
GOP leaders maintained that their decision to adjourn early was intended to allow members to return to their constituencies and campaign.
“It’s time for our members to go home to their districts and make their case to the American people,” Johnson said.
The House schedule change also delayed other legislative business.
Votes on Environmental Protection Agency regulations that had been planned for Thursday were moved to Wednesday afternoon before lawmakers departed, according to reports.
The Senate is expected to remain in session for another three weeks.
When House members return, Republican leaders are expected to move quickly to table Massie’s resolution.
Johnson predicted that the impeachment attempt would fail, but the delayed proceedings mean lawmakers will not have to publicly take a position on Hegseth until after voters have cast their midterm ballots.

sources.news_title: Rep. Thomas Massie forcing vote on Pete Hegseth's impeachment - The Pulse of NH
sources.text:
Rep. Thomas Massie forcing vote on Pete Hegseth’s impeachment
(WASHINGTON) -- Outgoing Republican Rep. Thomas Massie seized the House floor for more than an hour Tuesday afternoon, launching a long-shot effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth stemming from his controversial administration over the Pentagon, including the war in Iran.
After sending a news release announcing his intent to impeach Hegseth, Massie quickly appeared on the floor where he stood for more than 67 minutes reading the sweeping 34-page resolution with eight articles of impeachment aloud.
"Secretary Hegseth has acted in a manner contrary to his trust as Secretary of Defense and subversive of constitutional government, to the great prejudice of the cause of law and justice, and to the manifest injury of the people of the United States of America," Massie read from the resolution, contending that Hegseth will "remain a threat to civilians and the laws of war, the integrity of United States diplomacy, and the Constitution if allowed to remain in office, and has acted in a manner grossly incompatible with his duties and the rule of law."
"Peter Brian Hegseth thus warrants impeachment and trial, removal from office, and disqualification to hold and enjoy any office of honor, trust, or profit under the United States," the resolution states.
The Pentagon responded to Massie's move, defending Hegseth in a statement to ABC News.
"Secretary Hegseth has been a transformative leader for the Department of War," Pentagon press secretary Kingsley Wilson said in the statement, later adding that the "entire Department is unified behind the Secretary’s vision and will continue working to put our warfighters and America first."
The articles of impeachment against Hegseth include ignoring laws that minimize civilian casualties, administering an "unlawful war" in Yemen, ordering extrajudicial killings, suppressing free speech and kidnapping a sovereign leader -- alluding to the U.S. capture of Nicolas Maduro early this year.
"Frankly, I was concerned that Mike Johnson would end Congress again, like shorten even our already truncated work period if he found out I was doing this. So I shared the idea with nobody," Massie said.
Massie, a conservative who has gained a reputation as a constitutionalist through his seven terms in the House, lost a primary earlier this summer after Trump endorsed his opponent.
It's unclear whether the vote will succeed, given Republicans' narrow majority in the House. Speaker Mike Johnson can lose two Republican votes before a third defection upsets the majority.
Unless GOP leaders change the floor schedule again, the House must hold a vote on the resolution within two-legislative days -- by Thursday, which would force Republicans to go on the record defending Hegseth ahead of the high-stakes midterm elections. GOP leaders could offer a motion to table the resolution or cancel the legislative session scheduled for Thursday to avoid the vote.
Speaking to reporters afterward, Massie explained that he introduced the articles of impeachment to place a "marker" in history on what he said was both President Donald Trump's and Hegseth's "illegal" conduct.
“Doing this wasn't predicated on whether it could succeed or not; there needs to be a marker in history,” Massie said. "The president has exceeded, and Secretary Hegseth specifically, in many ways himself, and sometimes directed by illegal orders from the president, they have exceeded all norms for rules of engagement for how you use or misuse our military, to take oil from another country, to kidnap a foreign leader, like somebody needs to put a marker in history, and that's what this is. Hopefully, it passes, and they can litigate this in the Senate.”
Massie also told ABC News he had waited until Tuesday because it presents the last possible time to force consideration of a privileged resolution Congress before the midterms.
Massie added he felt he had exhausted all other legislative ways to stymie the war in Iran as well as other foreign military interventions.
"Why today? Because Speaker Johnson has basically canceled the rest of Congress until the elections," Massie explained. "Two days from now is the end of our session before we go on recess, and there can be a vote within two days. So I had to do it today."
